General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.
  • In a recent development, as Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs.
  • Recent findings suggest that but out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

In a recent development, as Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time. Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

Recent findings suggest that but out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Recent findings suggest that politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

According to recent reports, but somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

According to recent reports, this is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

In a recent development, so the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the….

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy.

1: The President Controls the Economy.

Recent findings suggest that if there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too major – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

The government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

2: The President Controls Interest Rates.

It has been revealed that this one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from upcoming jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it).

This line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

In a recent development, but most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Industry observers note that bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR indicated that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

4: The President Controls Housing Prices.

One vital thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, swiftly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are At the moment “High” and We Want Them Lower.

Recent findings suggest that ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive).

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, fresh EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About.

In a recent development, the funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Sources indicate that yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more promptly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

In a recent development, but have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

It has been revealed that and “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

But alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

In the Comments: Has the election season been getting you down, pumping you up, or just giving you a thorough dose of “Meh”?

According to recent reports, while researching economic stats for this article, I came across a quirky but informative series of videos called USA Facts by none other than former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. It seems that he had the same frustration as me: Americans are fighting over a bunch of opinions and misinformation without even bothering to look up the actual facts. So he made a well-produced series of videos that just share the facts without the baggage of political hype on top of them. I wish our politicians could do the same thing!

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

According to recent reports, the core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or Fresh Year's Eve.

According to recent reports, your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

In a recent development, the pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Recent findings suggest that hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

Industry observers note that world of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Industry observers note that this sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. #21787. Tech Report: Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1485 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A couple of years ago, Mr.
  • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • In a recent development, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

In a recent development, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

In a recent development, among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore upcoming places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

Industry observers note that with all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the substantial-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

Recent findings suggest that this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze blueprint in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

Industry observers note that when it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I presently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

In a recent development, but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

Recent findings suggest that but for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

18 Jobs for Retirees – What They Pay and When Social Security Holds Back Benefits

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (358 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pick retirement work by its pay, its schedule, and how it fits your Social Security claim.
  • In the year you reach full retirement age, 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, Social Security holds back $1 for every $3 you earn above $65,160.
  • Because withheld benefits are credited back at full retirement age, the test is about when to claim, not whether to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pick retirement work by its pay, its schedule, and how it fits your Social Security claim. Claim before full retirement age, and until the year you reach it, Social Security holds back $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 a year. Your check rises at that age to account for the months withheld.

In the year you reach full retirement age, 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, Social Security holds back $1 for every $3 you earn above $65,160. It counts only what you earn before the month you reach that age, and from that month on, your earnings no longer reduce your benefit.

Because withheld benefits are credited back at full retirement age, the test is about when to claim, not whether to work. A job that pays well above the limit is a reason to wait to claim, while one that pays less leaves your check untouched.

Social Security counts only pay from work toward the limit. That means wages, including bonuses, commissions, and vacation pay, or net profit if you’re self-employed. A pension, an annuity, interest, and investment income don’t count, so a retiree who consults while drawing a pension is tested on the consulting income alone.

Sources indicate that to check a job against the limit, multiply its hourly pay by the hours you plan to work. Tutoring 20 hours a week for 50 weeks at the $20.84 median comes to $20,840, under the $24,480 limit.

Before you take a job that will pay more than the limit, enter your expected pay in Social Security’s earnings test calculator to see how much it would hold back.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that open Axos Business Interest Checking for the cash your business keeps on hand to pay bills.
  • It has been revealed that money a business keeps in checking for payroll, rent, and supplier bills has to stay where it can be spent the day a bill comes due.
  • In a recent development, axos Bank released online on July 4, 2000, and is headquartered in San Diego, with offices in Las Vegas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that open Axos Business Interest Checking for the cash your business keeps on hand to pay bills. Keep a $5,000 average daily balance to skip the $10 monthly fee, and stay under $50,000 to earn its top rate of 1.01%. At $50,000, the whole balance earns 0.20%, so put larger reserves in a business savings account.

It has been revealed that money a business keeps in checking for payroll, rent, and supplier bills has to stay where it can be spent the day a bill comes due. Axos Business Interest Checking pays 1.01% APY, the annual percentage yield, on balances up to $49,999.99, with no minimum number of transactions or card purchases required to earn it. It also charges a $10 monthly fee unless its average daily balance for the month reaches $5,000. Once the balance reaches $50,000, the rate on the whole balance, not just the part above the line, drops to 0.20%.

In a recent development, axos Bank released online on July 4, 2000, and is headquartered in San Diego, with offices in Las Vegas. It reports more than $28.2 billion in assets, and its parent company, Axos Financial, trades on the Fresh York Stock Exchange as AX. The Better Business Bureau rates it A+. For small businesses it offers savings and two checking accounts, one that pays interest and one that doesn’t, plus payroll, card processing, and loans backed by the U.S. Small Business Administration through partner companies.

Three things decide whether the account is worth it: how its rate tiers work, what it costs to keep, and how money gets in and out of an online bank.

Axos doesn’t pay each tier’s rate on just the dollars in that tier. Its account agreement applies one daily rate to the balance, and its rate table sets that rate by the range the balance falls in, so a $50,000 balance earns 0.20% on every dollar.

Take the rates Axos posted on November 15, 2026, and a balance that holds steady for a year. A business with $49,999 in the account earns about $505. One with $50,000 earns about $100, and it would take more than $500,000 in the account to earn $505 again.

Industry observers note that the waiver runs on the month’s average, so the balance can dip under $5,000 for a few days around payroll without triggering the fee, as long as the month averages $5,000 or more. A month that falls short costs $10, while $5,000 earns about $4 a month at the rate Axos posted in November 2026.

The 100-item limit counts every debit, credit, and deposited check, so a business that pays many small bills or takes frequent payments can go over it in a busy month.

In a recent development, checks go in through the Axos app or by mail. Cash goes in at an ATM that takes deposits, using the business debit card. Axos asks customers not to mail cash, and a deposit at an ATM Axos doesn’t own may not be available until the fifth business day after it’s made.

Relying on ATMs for cash makes the account a poor fit for a shop that takes in cash every day. A business paid by card, check, or transfer has little cash to deposit.

Recent findings suggest that the account pays best on operating cash, the money that has to stay in checking anyway to cover the next month’s payroll, rent, and card bills. Reserves, the money beyond next month’s bills, earn more in Axos Business Premium Savings, which pays 3.50% APY on balances up to $4,999,999.99 against this account’s top rate of 1.01%, with no monthly fee or minimum opening deposit. Savings gives up some access in return, since Axos charges $0.30 for each item past 20 a month and can limit certain savings withdrawals to six a month.

It has been revealed that run the rates Axos posted on November 15, 2026, for a business with $60,000 at Axos, held for a year. Left in Business Interest Checking, the whole $60,000 earns the second tier’s rate, about $120. Kept as $20,000 in checking for bills and $40,000 in Premium Savings, the same money earns about $1,602, with $202 coming from checking and $1,400 from savings.

Axos Basic Business Checking pays no interest, but it reimburses two outgoing domestic wires a month. For a business that sends two, that saves $30 a month, and Interest Checking earns that much only on an average balance above about $35,600 at the November 2026 rate.

Recent findings suggest that deposits carry FDIC insurance, the federal guarantee on bank deposits, up to the standard $250,000. Every account a business holds at Axos under the same ownership, through any of its brands, counts toward that one limit.

Sources indicate that for balances above it, Axos offers Insured Cash Sweep through the IntraFi network, which splits deposits into amounts under $250,000 at other FDIC-insured banks and extends coverage up to $265 million. Axos indicates swept deposits earn interest but doesn’t publish the rate. The business keeps one relationship and one statement with Axos, a relationship manager sets it up, and the program’s limits and eligibility rules apply.

The account connects to QuickBooks, in its desktop and online versions, and to the desktop version of Quicken, syncing directly or through a file downloaded from Axos.

Sources indicate that support comes from business relationship managers, by phone at 844-678-2726 on weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific time, and through secure messages in online banking. Axos’s business support pages list no weekend phone hours.

Recent findings suggest that each business can open one Interest Checking account. Axos opens business accounts only for companies in the United States, and the business and each owner and signer need a physical address on file.

Industry observers note that axos Business Interest Checking is a good place for a business’s bill money and a poor place for its savings. Its strongest case is a business that keeps a steady $5,000 to $50,000 in checking, stays within 100 transactions a month, and rarely wires money out, since that business earns 1.01% on cash that would otherwise sit idle.

It’s the wrong account for a business that deposits cash daily, sends several wires a month, or lets its balance run past $50,000. Keep a month of bills in Interest Checking, below $50,000, and move the rest into Axos Business Premium Savings.

Axos ONE Review – High-Yield Savings When Your Deposits Qualify

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Open Axos ONE if your paycheck already arrives by direct deposit.
  • The national average rate is 0.39% APY, or annual percentage yield, according to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, so a better rate usually means a second bank, away from the checking account your paycheck lands in.
  • Recent findings suggest that axos Bank opened as Bank of Internet USA on July 4, 2000, one of the first banks built to run fully online, and took the Axos name in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open Axos ONE if your paycheck already arrives by direct deposit. Each month with at least $1,500 in direct deposits and an average checking balance of at least $1,500, savings earns 4.21% APY, and the bundle charges no monthly or overdraft fees. If your deposits vary month to month, pick a savings account that pays its rate without conditions.

Most banks pay little on savings. The national average rate is 0.39% APY, or annual percentage yield, according to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, so a better rate usually means a second bank, away from the checking account your paycheck lands in. Axos ONE pairs checking and high-yield savings at one online bank and ties the savings rate to the checking side. In any month the checking account meets its deposit and balance terms, savings earns the boosted rate. In a month it misses them, savings drops to 1.00% and checking earns nothing.

Recent findings suggest that axos Bank opened as Bank of Internet USA on July 4, 2000, one of the first banks built to run fully online, and took the Axos name in 2018. It’s based in San Diego, and its parent, Axos Financial, trades on the New York Stock Exchange and reported $30.8 billion in total assets at the end of September 2026. Axos also runs UFB Direct, which matters for the new-customer promotion and the deposit insurance below.

Axos ONE is two accounts opened together, and the checking account’s activity decides the rates on both.

Industry observers note that most of the bundle’s value is in savings. In a qualifying month it pays 4.21% APY on balances up to $249,999.99 and 3.50% on the portion above that. In any other month, the whole balance earns 1.00%.

Sources indicate that checking pays 0.51% APY in a qualifying month and nothing otherwise. There’s no monthly fee, no minimum balance, and no overdraft or nonsufficient-funds fee. A payment your balance can’t cover may still be paid or returned, just without a charge. A direct deposit can arrive up to two days early, depending on whether and when your payer funds it. The Visa debit card works fee-free at more than 95,000 ATMs, and Axos reimburses up to $10 a month in other banks’ domestic ATM fees.

The bank’s standalone Axos Checking pays 1.00% APY, a promotional rate, in any statement cycle with at least $1 in direct deposits, and reimburses domestic ATM fees without a cap, but it carries no savings boost. If you only need checking, Axos Checking or another free checking account without a balance requirement is the simpler choice.

Each month, the checking account must meet both halves of one option for either account to earn its boosted rate:.

Sources indicate that both accounts must also be open on the 25th and on the day interest is paid. A newly introduced account’s first window starts the day it opens, and one opened on or after the 25th starts qualifying the next month.

In a recent development, the fairest yardstick for those terms is Axos’s own Summit Savings, which pays 3.75% APY with no minimum balance and no monthly requirements. Take $20,000 kept in savings for a year at the rates Axos paid when this review was written. At 4.21%, qualifying every month earns about $842 in Axos ONE, $92 more than the $750 Summit Savings pays at 3.75%. At the 1.00% base rate, missing every month earns about $200, $550 less than Summit.

Sources indicate that latest customers who open the bundle by December 1, 2026 can earn 5.00% APY on up to $49,999.99 of savings for six statement cycles, the opening cycle included, or five when the account opens on or after the 25th. Each cycle still has to meet the monthly terms, and the boost is off in any cycle the savings balance averages $250,000 or more. Anyone who holds or has ever held an Axos Bank or UFB Direct account, loan, or investment is excluded, so opening another Axos account first, Summit Savings included, rules you out. At the rates when this review was written, the boost adds 0.79 percentage points, about $197 over six cycles on a full $49,999.99.

Recent findings suggest that the fees Axos ONE does charge cover less routine moves. Outgoing wires cost $35 within the U.S. and $45 abroad, incoming wires are free, and debit card purchases and ATM withdrawals in a foreign currency carry a 1% conversion fee.

According to recent reports, axos works online, so the app and the phone carry most of the load. Its Axos All-In-One Mobile Banking app holds a 4.7-star rating from about 20,000 ratings on Apple’s App Store, and a Direct Banker answers the phone 24/7, Thanksgiving and Christmas aside. Checks deposited by phone are held five days.

Cash is the awkward part. You can deposit it at participating ATMs or at the register of retailers in the Green Dot network, such as 7-Eleven, CVS, and Walmart. The store may charge up to $4.95 per deposit, and each deposit can run $20 to $500, more at Walmart and ACE Cash Express.

Deposits are insured by the FDIC through Axos Bank up to $250,000 per depositor in each ownership category, such as individual or joint. Money you keep at UFB Direct or any other Axos brand counts toward the same limit, since Axos insures them all under one FDIC certificate.

For larger savings, the Axos Insured Deposit Program moves money from Axos ONE Savings to partner banks, each insuring up to the same limit, for up to $2.5 million in additional coverage. Enrolling online or in the app is free and leaves your rate and features unchanged. Checking stays outside the program. You also can’t exclude a partner bank, and Axos leaves it to you to watch which banks hold your money, which matters if you already bank at one of them.

Axos ONE works best as a home for a paycheck that already arrives by direct deposit. That deposit, plus a $1,500 cushion in checking, earns savings the boosted rate, no part of the bundle charges a monthly or overdraft fee, and the extra FDIC coverage is free. For a saver who wants checking and savings at one bank, that’s a strong combination.

It’s a poor fit for freelancers and others whose deposits arrive irregularly and for anyone who can’t spare $1,500 in checking, since Summit Savings or another account with no monthly terms would earn them more. Savers who move money out often or deposit cash will run into its six-withdrawal limit and paid cash deposits. Readers whose paycheck clears $1,500 a month should open the bundle and point the direct deposit to its checking account so it posts by the 25th.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that open Axos Basic Business Checking if your business gets paid by card, bank transfer, or wire and you want no monthly fee, no minimum balance, and no cap on transactions.
  • Sources indicate that axos makes a small business choose between earning interest and avoiding fees.
  • In a recent development, axos has been a digital bank since it opened on July 4, 2000, and runs from its San Diego headquarters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that open Axos Basic Business Checking if your business gets paid by card, bank transfer, or wire and you want no monthly fee, no minimum balance, and no cap on transactions. Skip it if you deposit cash or paper checks often, since both can take until the fifth business day to become available.

Sources indicate that axos makes a small business choose between earning interest and avoiding fees. Its interest-bearing account, Axos Business Interest Checking, charges $10 in any month its average daily balance is under $5,000, plus 50 cents for each transaction past 100 a month. A business that keeps $5,000 there and stays at 100 transactions or fewer earns interest and pays neither fee. Basic Business Checking pays no interest and charges neither fee at any balance or transaction count.

In a recent development, axos has been a digital bank since it opened on July 4, 2000, and runs from its San Diego headquarters. It counts more than $28.2 billion in assets, and its parent tech giant, Axos Financial, trades on the New York Stock Exchange as AX. The Better Business Bureau, which has accredited Axos Bank since 2011, rates it A+.

Basic Business Checking’s strength is its short list of fees. Its weakness is getting cash and checks into the account, since Axos has only two branches.

Axos’s account page and its small-business fee schedule, effective September 28, 2026, set these terms:.

According to recent reports, electronic direct deposits are available the day Axos receives them, and incoming wires the next business day. Axos’s account agreement lets it hold other incoming ACH transfers, the standard electronic payments between bank accounts, for up to five business days after they post. The money may be released on the third business day if no payment is returned.

Checks go in through the app, up to 60 a month, $50,000 a business day, and $150,000 in any 30 days. Axos makes them available on the fifth business day after the deposit unless it releases them sooner, so a business paid mostly by check waits about a week for its money.

Cash is harder. In its March 2026 review of the bank, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency counted one branch in San Diego, with an ATM that takes deposits, and one in Las Vegas, which Axos’s agreement states accepts no cash. Elsewhere, cash goes in at other banks’ ATMs that accept deposits, which Axos’s ATM locator finds, and Axos makes it available by the fifth business day at the latest. A business that takes in cash every week should check for one near it before applying.

Axos’s app demonstrates business and personal Axos accounts under one login, moves money between them, and sends wires. Bill Pay comes with the account and usually delivers a payment by ACH in one to three business days, or as a mailed check in up to 10. Its limits are $100,000 for a payment to a company or a transfer, $10,000 to a person, and $2,500 by email, and Axos won’t raise them.

For bookkeeping, the account connects to QuickBooks Desktop, QuickBooks Online, and Quicken’s desktop version, either directly or through transaction files you download in CSV, QBO, QFX, or OFX format and import.

In a recent development, A growing business may outgrow the standard platform in two ways. It can’t yet add a user who isn’t a signer on the account, such as a bookkeeper or accountant, and it doesn’t send batches of ACH payments to staff or vendors. Both come with Axos’s treasury management service, its package of payment and fraud-control tools for businesses, which is free for a first account and charges $1 a batch and $1 for each ACH payment past 15 a month.

Recent findings suggest that axos Bank’s deposits carry Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) coverage up to $250,000 per depositor in each ownership category, the FDIC’s groups for how money is owned, under FDIC certificate 35546. A business that keeps more can ask a relationship manager to set up Axos’s Insured Cash Sweep, which places money at other banks in the IntraFi network and can raise coverage to $265 million, with interest paid on what’s swept.

Recent findings suggest that sole proprietors should add up their personal money too. The FDIC insures a sole proprietorship’s deposits as the owner’s own, combined with the owner’s other individual accounts at the same bank, and Axos’s UFB Direct brand counts as the same bank. A corporation’s or partnership’s deposits are insured in their own category.

Industry observers note that A business formed less than a year before it applies can earn up to $200 by applying with promo code START200 by January 31, 2027. Axos pays $50 for each statement cycle in which the account’s average daily balance is at least $3,000, in any four of its first five statement cycles, counting the month it opens.

The business must also never have been the primary owner of an Axos small-business account, and Axos closes the account if it isn’t approved and funded within 60 days. An account closed within 180 days can be charged up to $200 for closing early, and the bonus may be taxable and reported on a Form 1099.

The balance costs little to hold. At a sample savings rate of 3.50% annual percentage yield (APY), $3,000 would earn about $35 in four months, by our math. A business that can spare the balance gives up that $35 to collect up to $200.

Recent findings suggest that an established business can’t use START200, and Axos’s other cash offer needs a large savings balance. A business that pairs the account with Business Premium Savings, opening both in one application with code SBB600 by January 31, 2027, can earn up to $600. Axos pays $100 for each statement cycle in which the business meets four requirements by the 25th of the month. They are a $50,000 average daily balance in savings, a $1,500 average in checking, a deposit of $1,000 or more by ACH, wire, or check from outside Axos, and two debit card purchases of $50 or more.

Business Premium Savings pays 3.50% APY on balances under $5 million with no monthly fee, though it charges 30 cents for each transaction past 20 a month. Only one Axos offer applies to a business at a time.

Axos says its application takes minutes online. It opens accounts only for businesses in the United States, and every signer must live in the U.S., with a physical address there and a Social Security number, though citizenship isn’t required. The application asks for the business’s Employer Identification Number (EIN), a Social Security number for a sole proprietor, ownership agreements, a business license, and articles of incorporation or organization.

Axos may turn down businesses in industries it restricts, such as cannabis, cryptocurrency, internet gambling, or money services. It also can’t process an application while a freeze is in place at ChexSystems, a company that reports on checking account history, and it asks applicants to lift any TransUnion credit freeze first.

Help comes through one number, 844-678-2726. Relationship managers answer weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific time, and after hours, on weekends, and on holidays the line handles fraud alerts, card services, and urgent problems. The Visa debit card and any checks ordered with the application arrive in seven to 10 business days.

Axos Basic Business Checking costs close to nothing to run. It has no monthly fee, minimum, or transaction cap, it refunds other banks’ ATM fees, and it covers two outgoing wires a month, so a business paid by card, bank transfer, or wire pays little beyond overdrafts and extra wires.

A business that handles cash or paper checks every week will wait on its money, since both can take until the fifth business day to become available, and would do better at a bank with a branch nearby. One that keeps a large balance earns nothing here, where Axos’s Business Interest Checking or Business Premium Savings would pay interest. Freelancers and online businesses paid electronically should open it. A business formed within the past year should apply with code START200 by January 31, 2027, and keep $3,000 in it for four of its first five statement cycles to collect the full $200.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Starting with your 2026 return, you can deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts to eligible charities while taking the standard deduction, or $2,000 on a joint return.
  • The IRS’s Working Families Tax Cuts page says, “Beginning with tax year 2026, individuals who do not itemize may deduct up to $1,000 of cash contributions made to eligible charitable organizations ($2,000 for married taxpayers filing jointly).” It’s permanent, unlike the temporary version for 2020 and 2021.
  • Recent findings suggest that two words in that rule decide which gifts count.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting with your 2026 return, you can deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts to eligible charities while taking the standard deduction, or $2,000 on a joint return. Give by check, card, or bank transfer straight to the charity, since donated goods, stock, and gifts to donor-advised funds don’t count. Keep a bank record or receipt for every gift.

The IRS’s Working Families Tax Cuts page says, “Beginning with tax year 2026, individuals who do not itemize may deduct up to $1,000 of cash contributions made to eligible charitable organizations ($2,000 for married taxpayers filing jointly).” It’s permanent, unlike the temporary version for 2020 and 2021.

Recent findings suggest that two words in that rule decide which gifts count. The first, cash, means money, given in bills or by check, card, bank transfer, or payroll deduction. Clothing, stock, and other property don’t count, and neither do deductions carried over from earlier years.

The second, eligible, rules out some gifts of money. Donations to a supporting organization, a charity set up to support other charities, don’t count, and neither do donations to a donor-advised fund, which only itemizers can deduct.

Industry observers note that look each charity up in the IRS’s Tax Exempt Organization Search. Its deductibility code reads PC for a public charity, which qualifies, and starts with SO for a supporting organization. A church can qualify without appearing there. For every gift, keep a bank record or receipt showing the charity’s name, the date, and the amount, plus the charity’s written acknowledgment for any single gift of $250 or more.

Say a married couple in the 12% bracket takes the standard deduction and gives $150 a month by card, split between their church and a food bank. That’s $1,800 for 2026, all deductible under the $2,000 limit on a joint return, so their tax drops by $216. Since no single gift reaches $250, their card statements are all the records they need.

From 2026, itemizers can deduct only the part of their gifts above 0.50% of adjusted gross income. If your itemized deductions come close to the standard deduction, count your gifts both ways before you take the standard deduction or itemize, and consider bunching two years of gifts into a year you itemize.

Recent findings suggest that make a gift by Dec. 31 for it to count on that year’s return. A mailed check counts the day you mail it, and a card gift in the year it’s charged, not the year you pay the bill.

#21747. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2567 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
  • The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
  • This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

It has been revealed that is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

It has been revealed that “The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

Industry observers note that if the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Industry observers note that now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a significant Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

Sources indicate that this is exactly why the price of an individual firm’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

But what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more swiftly?

Recent findings suggest that in the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 substantial companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

According to recent reports, these are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

There’s one common theme in the big tech manufacturer boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

According to recent reports, but that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

They may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

According to recent reports, as I remarked earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

Sources indicate that everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

In a recent development, just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

Industry observers note that it’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

What About Paying Off Your House?

Industry observers note that over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Industry observers note that another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Sources indicate that then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

In the Comments: what are your thoughts on the current stock market boom, future crashes and busts, and the role of Artificial Intelligence in our future?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

In a recent development, rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many consumers like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Users who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

According to recent reports, pocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

Monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Users often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Users who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

It has been revealed that if you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused users or those who prefer full manual control.

Sources indicate that subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android users. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android consumers.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and plan better for annual vs monthly charges.

Subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

It has been revealed that call the charity or check its website before you drop off used stuff, since it has to pay to throw out anything it can’t sell or use. Bring only clean, working, complete items, and get a dated receipt that lists each one, which backs up a tax deduction if you itemize.

Goodwill Northern Latest England notes it has to throw away old air conditioners, mattresses, and anything else it can’t sell, and the cost comes out of the money for its programs.

It has been revealed that some things are off limits by law. The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) notes it’s illegal to sell any recalled product. Many thrift stores also turn away car seats and old tube TVs, and each charity sets its own list.

Sources indicate that one call can change where everything goes. A couple clearing out a parent’s home calls the family shelter nearby and learns it needs kitchen basics and bedding but has no use for clothes. The clothes go to a thrift store whose sales fund a job program instead.

Drop things off during open hours and leave with a dated receipt. List each item on it, since the IRS asks for a description of what you gave, then keep it with your tax papers in case you itemize deductions.

Fuel Surcharges on Promo Awards.

It has been revealed that picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points people miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

Recent findings suggest that flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you initiative a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.
